idiom_name: protocol implementor held as any Renderer (existential) or as a generic
implementation_notes: The implementor is a protocol and the abstraction holds it either as a boxed protocol type (any Renderer - an existential with a heap box and indirect dispatch) or as a generic parameter or opaque result type (some Renderer - static dispatch, no box). Apple's documentation of existential types states the trade explicitly: existentials buy runtime flexibility and heterogeneous collections, while generics, opaque types, concrete types or enums avoid boxing and dispatch costs. The protocol therefore replaces the abstract Implementor base, and an existential is the direct analogue of the classic pointer to an implementor; generics are preferred whenever a single concrete type suffices. Protocols with Self or associated-type requirements cannot be used as any existentials at all, so design the implementor protocol without them if runtime substitution is required.
code_sketch:
protocol Renderer { func circle(_ r: Double) }   // Implementor
struct CircleShape {                             // Abstraction (boxed implementor)
    let renderer: any Renderer
    let radius: Double
    func draw() { renderer.circle(radius) }      // dynamic dispatch through the box
}

struct CircleShapeGeneric<R: Renderer> {         // static dispatch, no box
    let renderer: R
    let radius: Double
    func draw() { renderer.circle(radius) }
}
pitfalls: any P boxes the value and dispatches indirectly; Apple's guidance is to refactor hot paths to concrete, generic, opaque or enum types, so an existential in an inner loop pays for the flexibility twice.
A protocol with Self or associated-type requirements cannot be used as an existential at all, so it cannot serve as the implementor type for runtime substitution.
some P as a return type must be a single concrete type on every path, so it cannot hide which implementor was chosen - that is a compile error, not a design option.
